posts.title: Modular Building Sets - Rumours and Discussion
posts.text: You wrote a great description. The first batch of modulars have a sort of "grandeur" with their rather simple building techniques. Palace Cinema was the first of the Creator Expert Era but I'd argue it sort of carries this as well. The building techniques starting getting a bit more complicated and detailed with those ones. The current era started with the Police Station in 2021 (the first with the black box art) and designs have gotten even more complex with it.

posts.title: Modular Building Sets - Rumours and Discussion
posts.text: The first modular I bought was green grocer when it came out. I now own all but 4 modulars, however, this year's Shopping Street I didn't build but instead built Briquoleur's High Street Therapist alt-build. So like 3½ I don't own. I think your ranking also can be looked at this way... Early modulars were putting toes in the water trying out the concept and see if it worked. Everything since then has evolved with new pieces, creative designs with angles, etc. So in the middle time frame, things became more advanced with newer pieces. And in the last 5 or 6 years, the number of new pieces, as well as the creativity of what we can do with those pieces has exploded, making really detailed builds. Starting with the Boutique Hotel, 3 of the last 5 modulars have been angle-driven, which leads to lots of creativity. I mentioned BrickAtive's Cafe Fleur. That felt like a master-class in angles. It is a corner building but features 4 distinct sides instead of the 2 that a squared-off building would have on the street sides. Plotting it out for putting it in my town was a nightmare but it looks great now. TLDR version: as the available pieces expanded, the details of modulars has improved. I hated the dark azure bottom of the Jazz Club, so I built mine with bright pink bottom instead. So everything dark azure is bright pink. Also, the brown 1x1 tiles, I used bright pink. Looks much better IMO. I tried a few other complementary colors as well on the tiles and found bright pink to be the best fit.

posts.title: Modular Building Sets - Rumours and Discussion
posts.text: I love the Fire Brigade, but it's not a great modular. Palace Cinema and earlier all seem much simpler to me (although I don't have Town Hall, Market Street, or Cafe Corner). Green Grocer is nicely detailed, but feels too large in comparison with all the others (especially the more recent buildings). Palace Cinema is a fun concept, but very basic inside and the outside isn't that special. Fire Brigade brings me great joy to look at, but it also shows it's age. Parisian Restaurant to Assembly Square are all good. They are all nice builds, have terrific play features and stories. They look solid. All of them classics. Downtown Diner was a revelation. I know it's looks are divisive, but it's what got me into modulars, having ignored them before. I love the look and the build is awesome. From there they are generally all terrific, with some rising more than others. Boutique Hotel had me laughing with delight at some of the techniques. Tudor Corner is incredible. But as we move to later modulars, they start to get that little bit smaller, and are comically smaller compared to Green Grocer. But I still favour them over the earlier ones. I would like to see a modular in the new warm pink. I think it could be a great colour for something classic. Earth Blue might also make a nice option for the right style (they tried Jazz Club in it and felt it was cold, which a lot of people disagreed with upon release, but I think they're right). Agreed. I'd love some of the dramatic Parisian-style buildings, and Cafe Fleur is on my list to get parts for at some point soon. It's a terrific looking model and the curve of the roof is great. The whole thing would look great in tan, but I still like the colour blocking of nougat, white, and dark orange.

posts.title: So, what Do people want?
posts.text: Agreed that the real challenge is in designing our own builds and making it work. Official sets can be challenging exactly by making instructions not too easy. That doesn't have to be frustrating. If I look at the old 8880 Super Car, the whole car was made in 36 main steps over 50 pages. Was it hard? No. But you had to pay closer attention than in modern times, because we weren't being held hands as much as nowadays and there'd be more parts per instruction step. Was it frustrating to spot the differences? Not once you learned how things worked and paid attention. Did we have to backtrack? No, because advanced Technic models always had the parts and amounts listed per step just like every model has nowadays. So if you thought you were done and had parts left over, you knew you missed something.

posts.title: LEGO Star Wars Set Discussion 2026 - READ FIRST POST!!!
posts.text: I get the impression that it’s one of the elements of the canon that the book writers or Story Group had to come up with to justify why the galaxy was woefully unprepared for the First Order. One of the many examples of them having to play catch-up with JJ Abrams and Lawrence Kasdan wanting to reset the state of the Galaxy for nostalgia’s sake. Luke’s overall mentality and mindset as a Jedi is another victim of this IMO, Legends was practically filled with examples of him learning from the old Order’s mistakes whilst canonically, he practically mirrored their ethos. I still feel the whiplash of that all these years later as one of Lucasfilm’s biggest mistakes. I know my response is a little sensationalist, but I genuinely think they’re too busy huffing their own Rhydonium and making broad assumptions on what they think people want out of Lego Star Wars rather than just trying to gauge what’s actually in demand. Of course there’s no universally accepted list of what people want from the theme, but there are enough platforms out there and plenty of recurring patterns of what people have been asking for that’s it’s not difficult to secure some easy wins that they simply refuse to do for whatever reason. I’m being somewhat hypocritical because certain things we’re getting next year like Cloud City, a General Anakin figure, and so on are things people have been asking for, so it’s not like they’re completely oblivious to what people want I guess. Yeah I can understand that, hope you’ve been keeping well in the interim man. This is the double-edged sword of leaked lists releasing uncharacteristically early I guess, it just drives that feeling of a drought pretty quickly soon after. Makes me wonder how it feels to be the Lucasfilm rep that presents all the awesome concept art from these new shows to Lego only for them to be disregarded entirely. What annoys me most is how often Lego actively overlook things that flat-out make for good toys in favour of experimental things literally no one has asked for, which more often than not don’t end up selling well anyway. Then again, Star Wars is one of Lego’s most profitable themes so perhaps that drives a more hands-off approach from Lucasfilm when it comes to their choice of sets. Yeah I haven’t bought a Studio Series figure since AoE Leader Optimus last year. That said, whenever they get around to covering Transformers: Prime in Studio Series, I will truly have no recourse but to buy them. As much non-transforming transformers don’t appeal to me, I bought the Blokees Action-class Optimus Prime from TF: One and holy cow is that thing awesome. On the Transformers front, I saw that Studio Series TLK Leader Megatron is priced at £65. Wild. Apologies, back to Lego Star Wars. If I recall, this year’s January wave was revealed last December. I have a feeling the 2027 winter wave reveal will occur much earlier this year (hopefully start of November) due to the 50th anniversary angle. Fingers crossed for a juicy press release soon.

posts.title: Cylinder advice
posts.text: My personal experience is that some of the specialty Technic beams are the best way to model steam cylinders, like the 3x3 "T" shaped Technic beam. My 2-6-0 model below uses this part, and to give credit where credit is due, my idea to use Technic beams for this purpose is borrowed from Tony Sava: Even though this model is of a prototype that is smaller than the PRR I1sa, my model is built in a larger scale (1:38, 10-wide.) Doing some rough math, in 1:48 scale my assembly would be about as close to scale as Lego gets for the I1sa's cylinders, so borrowing the idea and basic dimensions should work for your model. Hopefully this helps!

posts.title: Lego Blockly: Graphical Common Programming Environment Web App (Using Intuitive Blockly) for All Lego Robotic Platforms.
posts.text: Of course! They all work perfectly well - even with the ancient TSOP 38438. I added two Serial.print() lines to your firmware code, and checked whether the code decided it is PF IR or generic IR. I also had my oscilloscope hooked up to ESP GPIO 16 - the 38438 usually does pick-up some digital "noise", but that is easily taken care of. Also, 38438 easily saturates when the remotes, particularly the PF handsets, are too close, but this is all old knowledge. The PF remotes blow out quite the IR radiation, as users wanted to go as far away as possible. But then you need to use modern versions of the TSOP IR sensors. I just had my old but good 38438 in stock ;) The cheap strip remotes are most reliably detected by the ESP - these remotes run on CR2032 3V button cells - and thus don't blow out Watts of IR radiation. Which gives a lot of "key freedom"!!! Best Thorsten

posts.text: That is again a nice find @amine!!! These NIVO/CMA UIA/B cards are really powerful PC I/O cards. As there were many, back in the days! And as said before, regarding Int.A these cards are totally overblown: 2 full 8-bit programmable digital I/O ports (via the 8255 PIO), 4 channel analog in, and some advanced control lines ... so this is why they were widely used in the NL (and elsewhere) classrooms: You could sample a myriad of sensors (provided by CMA as well - and of course any type of homebrew versions!) - that was true for myriads of cards/extensions/cartridges for all the 8-bit wonders flooding the 1980's. The "difference" is that CMA also provided school curricula, is that correct? Most importantly: LEGO did endorse these cards, as they provided the files, to configure such a powerful card, is that correct? Using 9771, you need to "configure" >one< soldered bridge - I bet only a tiny number of teachers clipped that bridge, to run programs on the second I/O address. Using BASIC, COMAL, etc. - as TCLogo as well as LEGO Lines don't know how to use the alternative address (as shown here). They just use the primary (bridge intact) address. To me, it looks like the UIA and UIB cards are OK with Int.A, but that was only one out of so many other options/interfaces/sensors? Best Thorsten

posts.text: Well, thats the point @evank I've contacted CMA today because this link describes their UIA card. The NIVO-card controlling Interface A mentioned on several places in documentation = the CMA UIA-card. At first 500 were made under the name NIVO, after that about 5000 were sold under the CMA name. CMA made the measurement software Coach, which also supports controlling Lego interface A. In their reaction they state they can still supply software and license of Coach5. It would cost €20 ex. Interesting though that I'm not the only one contacting them about this. In the response they state that at least three requests have been made this month. Worst part of the story is that in 1997 when I started working in educuation I've installed several Coach5 instances and we had the UIA. After CMA abbandonded it (as stated in the post of @amine) we discarded these cards and the software/license. If only had known back then. <Mail from info@cma-science.nl> We hebben een zip-folder met de applicatie Coach 5 Lego en kunnen nog licenties aanmaken. Zelf kunnen we het niet draaien en we geven dan ook geen garantie of ondersteuning. Wel hebben (internationaal) tenminste 3 liefhebbers het deze maand werkend gekregen. Ben je hierin geïnteresseerd, stuur dan je volledige naam en adresgegevens voor een proforma voor €20 excl BTW. Na betaling krijg je dan de file (ca 7MB) en login. posts.title: Prytz / Hatchet Planimeter (Free instructions)
posts.text: A Prytz / Hatchet Planimeter, made in 2013, now with free PDF instructions in an updated and improved version. If you want to learn measuring areas with LEGO, this is the tool you need ! This article is a transcript of the presentation video on Youtube (3min) : Model Presentation Measuring the surface area of an irregular shape usually requires digital software or complex geometric formulas. However, it can also be done mechanically using this device called a planimeter. It enables calculates the area of any flat shape simply by tracing its perimeter and I have made a version using LEGO Technic part. The model consists of three main components : First, the tracer arm at the bottom, which features a fine yellow pointer used to follow the lines of the drawing Second, the wheel arm, equipped with a grippy LEGO tire that acts as a directional guide tangent wheel Third, a custom dial calibrated to display the surface area directly in square centimeters (cm²) To use it, fold the mechanism, reset the needle to zero, and place the pointer on a starting reference mark. Then trace the contour of the shape. Once you return to the starting point, the needle on the dial indicates the total area. How does it work ? Without going too deep into the mathematics, the calculation relies on a geometric curve known as a tractrix and Green’s Theorem. Due to the friction of the tire, the rear wheel cannot slip sideways : it is constrained to either roll forward and backward or pivot around its center. As the pointer follows the perimeter of a shape, the wheel arm traces a tractrix. This physical trajectory dynamically computes a line integral, which Green’s Theorem translates directly into a surface area. This is why you see the dial numbers increase when traveling along the upper section of the shape, and then decrease when traveling along the bottom. What the mechanism does is subtract the bottom area from the upper area, leaving only the enclosed space inside the curve. Green’s Theorem However, on this specific model, the dial is not driven directly by a rolling wheel like on an Amsler polar planimeter. Instead, the wheel arm is mechanically linked to the dial so that its angular position is reported directly on the dials. If the shape remains small relative to the arm length, the angular deviation between the two positions is directly proportional to the area. It works exactly like the small-angle approximation in trigonometry, where sinus alpha approx alpha when it is small. The device uses this geometry to approximate the area, and the internal gearing system multiplies this angle to display it on the reading dial (with the inherent error due to gear backlash). If you want to go deeper in the mathematics explanations, you can read the article on the blog and read these resources : Wikipedia page about planimeter (general) Different Hatchet Planimeters by David R Green on uraone.com Deeper explanations with Mathematics by Robert L. Foote (persweb.com) 2026 Version (updated and improved) - Free Instructions This is the second version of the device, initially built in 2013, redesigned to improve the original build, here are the changes : Better accuracy : The yellow pointer is now much smaller, allowing for more precise tracking along line edges Reduced friction : The tangent wheel is now free to move on its axle, as well as the yellow pointer to follow the hands rotation Quick calibration : The axle of the needle is now with friction, which enables to rotate and set up easily to zero The major improvement is that I have made the PDF building instructions for this device, and that it is available for free, with the dial and the measuring sheet to print. 📲 https://www.nico71.fr/product/prytz-hatchet-planimeter/ 🧩 https://rebrickable.com/mocs/MOC-278151/Nico71/prytz-hatchet-planimeter/#parts (custom dial to print as well and measuring sheet used in the video to be printed on A4 size, 100% scale).

posts.title: Lego Blockly: Graphical Common Programming Environment Web App (Using Intuitive Blockly) for All Lego Robotic Platforms.
posts.text: Thank you! Just "soldered" my ESP32 PFIR BLE server - this is in reference to @Bliss post/update in the general thread about "Programs to allow interaction between old LEGO Control Interfaces", @Bliss post about the ESP PF IR, September 11, 2026. I decided to "lift" the IR components (a TSOP 34838 for IR RX and an LD274 for IR TX) to the component side of the ESP board, which is, as usual ;) an ESP32 WROOM-32 DevKit1. This way, the USB (power) connector does not get in the way of IR traffic light - and I can look at the beautiful component side of the board while playing . The 5 extra components (2xIR, 1k+47 Ohm resistors, 2N5551 transistor) are soldered to a double-sided, pre-tinned scrap piece of perfboard. This piece was just lying around in the shop as well as a bunch of 2N5551; the TSOP is from 2010 - back then, I ordered a bunch of them for my (train) IRRF transceivers. The newer versions (TSOP 32438, 34438) are better suited as they eliminate almost all interfering light other than 38kHz modulated light, but hey, the old fellas work fine! Forgot: You can still press both the EN as well as the BOOT button. EN: Use a pencil or the like. BOOT: just "press" the TSOP, its connection is rather bendible). Below: Line-up of my current (mobile) ESP boards for @Bliss LEGO Blockly - from left to right: ESP32 for the Interface A (+ optionally PFIR TX, I have not installed the IR LED though, as this is done by the dedicated ESP PFIR board). ESP32 for PFIR RX+TX; RX includes PF IR codes sent by the two PF remotes/handsets as well as generic IR codes sent by 38kHz IR remotes. I have quite a number of these >very< cheap thingies. I can now control every LEGO device supported by LEGO Blockly using these. ESP32 for the Bluetooth Battery Cubes of the Tenka Circuit Cube product line. Each ESP board supports two cubes. This is just the bare-bone ESP board, as nothing else is required - it all works via Bluetooth LE (connection to PC/Blockly and to the Tenka Cubes. I should add something cool - maybe an OLED display or the like ;) Thank you, Yves!!! All the best Thorsten

posts.text: Oh, that's a tough one. I am not aware of anyone posting a detailed "how to" or "this is what I did" about that job. One of the trickiest things about the conversion that you are doing is that you have to think about both the upstream and downstream power on all four branches. Making it a lot easier to wind up with a dead spot, a short circuit, or both. I have no general advice beyond the following, I bet if you sat down with a pen and paper while looking at the layout you are fitting it into, you could figure out all of the potential dead spots and short circuits as you step through the 2^4 = 16 possible combinations of the switch positions

posts.title: So, what Do people want?
posts.text: I guess the answer there is to build as many LEGO sets as you can as there will be examples of all the building techniques they use. You don't even really need to build them. If I see something interesting in a set, I often download the instructions and look at how they did that thing. Building LEGO is a skill like any other skill. The more you build, the more you learn. The more you design yourself, the more you find your own style. I assume this is the point behind and why they continue to make the 'bucket' style sets. The instructions show how to build a few often simple designs but the idea is that you then use those techniques to build whatever you like. Although of course they are aimed at the younger age group. At least here in the UK, there are plenty of HOWTO type LEGO books, showing building ideas for getting started with a pile of bricks rather than using official instructions.
